notes.meaning: Israel had no king, so people mostly did as they liked. The tribe of Dan had been given land, but strong neighbors pushed them up into the hills. They never took all of it. So one part of the tribe went looking for a new home somewhere else. Many see this chapter as the private sin of one home in chapter 17 now spreading to a whole tribe.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars point to Judges 5:17 and say this story must come from early in the judges' time. They think the wording about land that had 'fallen' to Dan by lot was added by a later writer.

notes.meaning: The Danites sent five brave men to scout the land for the whole group. It was wise to look before they leaped. On the way north the men stopped for the night at Micah's house in the hills of Ephraim.

The spies knew the young Levite's voice. A Levite was a member of the tribe set apart to serve at God's house. Maybe they had met him before, or maybe they heard he had an accent from somewhere else. He told them Micah had hired him as his priest. One preacher said that a man who had already sold himself was easy to buy.

The spies asked Micah's priest to find out from God whether their trip would go well. They had passed by Shiloh, where God's true priest could have answered them. Instead they went to a man-made shrine. The Levite's answer sounded hopeful, but commentators call it empty and vague, like the answers pagan shrines gave. A prayer for success that does not bow to God's will cannot make a wrong plan right. And success alone does not prove God is pleased.

differ.view: A leading early Methodist commentator thought the answer truly came from the LORD. Because it came true, he believed Micah's worship was not idol worship. He called it unfair to say the answer was a trick.

notes.meaning: The spies reached Laish in the far north. The people there felt safe and lived at ease. They had no ruler to keep order, they were far from the city of Sidon, and they had no friends nearby to help them. Laish may have been a small settlement of people from Sidon. Its people felt secure, but they were not safe, and that made them easy to attack.

Back home, the spies urged the people to stop sitting still and go take this rich, wide land. They said God had given it to them. But that claim rested only on the answer from Micah's priest. One older commentator also uses these verses as a picture of heaven. It is a good land where nothing is lacking, so we should not be slow to lay hold of it.

Six hundred armed men set out, bringing their families and animals with them. They camped near Kiriath-jearim in Judah. The place was later called Mahaneh-dan, meaning 'camp of Dan,' and it is also named in Samson's story. Sadly, Dan could gather fighters for Laish but would not fight for the land God first gave them.

On the way north they came to Micah's place, which was really a small village. The spies told the others about Micah's shrine. It held an ephod (a special priest's vest used to ask God questions), household gods, and two idols. 'Think about what you should do' meant 'Don't miss this chance to get a shrine for our new home.'
The spies went to the Levite and greeted him in a friendly way. Meanwhile the six hundred armed men stood at the gate. The friendly greeting was cover for a robbery.

While the priest stood at the gate with the soldiers, the five spies went in and took everything from the shrine. When the priest saw it, he asked what they were doing. These 'gods' could not even keep themselves from being stolen. One preacher said it was mad for men to steal what they worshipped and then worship what they stole. Their religion began with breaking the command not to steal.

'Put your hand over your mouth' meant 'Be quiet.' The Danites offered the Levite a bigger job, as priest to a whole tribe instead of one family. 'Father' was a title of respect for a priest. The priest was glad. His hope for more honor and money crushed any loyalty to Micah. He took the sacred objects and walked in the middle of the group. That may have copied how the priests and the ark (the sacred chest holding God's law) traveled in the wilderness.
The Danites put their children, animals and valuables in front. They expected Micah to chase them from behind. Bringing their families and goods showed they never planned to come back.

Micah's neighbors gathered and caught up with the slow-moving group. They were probably people who also used his shrine. The Danites turned and asked Micah what his problem was, as if they had done nothing wrong.

Micah cried that they had taken the gods he made and his priest, so what did he have left? How foolish to call something you made yourself your god! The verse also warns us. Anything we feel we cannot live without becomes an idol. We should feel this way only about the true God. Idol worshippers carry their gods, but God carries His people.

differ.view: A leading early Methodist commentator held that Micah worshipped the true God. To him, 'my gods' means holy objects that stood for God's presence, not idols.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars say the word could be read 'my God,' and that Micah thought he was worshipping the LORD.

notes.meaning: The Danites threatened to kill Micah and his family if he kept complaining. This was simply 'might makes right,' like a robber saying 'your money or your life.' Micah saw they were too strong and went home. He turned away from the Danites when he should have turned back to the LORD. Losing our idols can be a great gain if it cures us of loving them.

The Danites attacked Laish, a quiet people who did not expect it. They killed them and burned the city. No one came to help, because Sidon was far away and Laish had no allies. Some commentators think the writer repeats 'quiet and unsuspecting' to show how cruel this was. Others point out that God had given this land to Israel. The Danites then rebuilt the city and settled there.

They renamed the city Dan after their ancestor. Living so far from the rest of their tribe, the name reminded everyone they still belonged to Israel. Dan became the northern edge of the land, so 'from Dan to Beersheba' came to mean all of Israel.

The Danites set up the stolen idol. Their priest, Jonathan, came from the family of Moses. That probably means a grandson or later descendant. Jewish copyists later added a small letter to make the name read 'Manasseh,' to spare Moses the shame. Sadly, the children of great and godly people can go astray. 'The captivity of the land' is hard to pin down. Many link it to the time the Philistines captured the ark, and others to Israel's later exile.

Micah's idol stayed at Dan the whole time God's house stood at Shiloh. This became a rival place of worship. Being far from Shiloh was Dan's excuse, and it kept the wrong worship going for a long time. It may be why King Jeroboam later chose Dan for one of his golden calves. It all began with one man's private shrine, which shows how a small fire can spread.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verse 31 was written by a different hand than verse 30. They see the two endings as the endings of two stories joined together.

problems: v. 31: dropped differ point (Methodist): no checkable source
